title: Independent study: interest rates and business (1.6.3)
subject: Business
unit: Spring 1: The international economy and government (1.5, 1.6)
source: Written for business/y10 lesson 31 (Pupil PDF: independent study, interest rates (1.6.3) with the Islamic note)
intro: Read this sheet, then answer the questions. Interest rates are taught as knowledge of how the wider economy works, never as something to take.

panels.title: Islamic note
panels.text: Riba (رِبَا) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba). Islamic finance uses partnership (mushārakah, مُشَارَكَة) and cost-plus sale (murābaḥah, مُرَابَحَة) instead.

panels.title: What is the interest rate?
points: The cost of borrowing money and the reward for saving in the conventional economy, set by banks, guided by the Bank of England base rate.
It changes how much people and businesses spend.

panels.title: When interest rates rise
points: Loans and overdrafts cost more, so firms with debt have higher costs and less profit.
Consumers with mortgages and loans have less to spend, so demand for luxuries falls.
Saving becomes more attractive than spending.
Firms delay investment in new machines and buildings.

panels.title: When interest rates fall
points: Borrowing is cheaper, so consumers spend more and demand rises.
Firms' costs of existing debt fall.
Exporters may gain if the pound weakens.

questions.q: Explain how a rise in interest rates could affect a furniture shop. (3)
questions.a: Customers with loans and mortgages have less money to spend (point), furniture is a big purchase that can be delayed (development), so the shop's sales and revenue fall (development).

questions.q: Give one reason a business with no debt may still be affected by higher interest rates.
questions.a: Its customers spend less because their own borrowing costs more, so demand falls.

questions.q: Name the two Islamic finance methods on this sheet and say what each means.
questions.a: Mushārakah: a partnership sharing profit and loss. Murābaḥah: a cost-plus sale at a fixed, agreed price.
